casadi::Callback Class Reference

User-defined Function implemented by subclassing. More...

#include <callback.hpp>

Detailed Description

A Callback is a Function whose numerical evaluation (and optionally its derivatives) is written by the user in Python, MATLAB or C++ by overriding virtual methods. It can be called like any Function, embedded in MX graphs, mapped, and used inside NLPs and integrators.

A subclass must call the base constructor and then construct(name, opts) from its own constructor; construct() queries the virtual methods below (get_n_in, get_n_out, get_sparsity_in/out, get_name_in/out) and calls init() and finalize(), so all data those methods need must be set before construct() runs. Only eval() is mandatory. Defaults: one scalar input "i0" and one scalar output "o0".

Object lifetime: the Function side holds a raw pointer to the user object and does not own it. The user must keep the Callback object alive (in Python: keep a reference) for as long as any Function, expression or solver that uses it exists; otherwise evaluation fails with "Callback object has been deleted". The same holds for objects returned from get_jacobian/get_forward/get_reverse. Callback objects cannot be copied.

Derivatives: by default a Callback is not differentiable, so jacobian(), forward/reverse sweeps and NLP solvers that need gradients fail with "Derivatives cannot be calculated". Either override has_jacobian/get_jacobian, has_forward/get_forward or has_reverse/get_reverse, or pass the option "enable_fd": True to construct() to use finite differences ("fd_method": "central" (default), "forward", "backward" or "smoothing"; "fd_options" such as {"h": 1e-6} tune the step). A user-provided Jacobian is itself differentiated with finite differences only when it is a Callback with "enable_fd"; a Function built from SX/MX gives exact second derivatives.

>>> class MyCallback(Callback):
...   def __init__(self, name, d, opts={}):
...     Callback.__init__(self)
...     self.d = d
...     self.construct(name, opts)
...   def get_n_in(self): return 1
...   def get_n_out(self): return 1
...   def eval(self, arg):
...     return [sin(self.d*arg[0])]
>>> f = MyCallback("f", 0.5)
>>> f
Callback(f:(i0)->(o0) CallbackInternal)
>>> f(2)
DM(0.8415)
>>> x = MX.sym("x")
>>> f(x)
MX(f(x){0})
>>> try:
...   jacobian(f(x), x)
... except Exception as e:
...   print("Derivatives cannot be calculated for f" in str(e))
True
>>> f = MyCallback("f", 0.5, {"enable_fd": True})
>>> J = Function("J", [x], [jacobian(f(x), x)])
>>> J(2)
DM(0.2702)


>> c = {'classdef MyCallback < casadi.Callback', 'properties', 'd', 'end', 'methods'};
>> c = [c, {'function self = MyCallback(name, d, varargin)'}];
>> c = [c, {'self@casadi.Callback(); self.d = d; construct(self, name, varargin{:});'}];
>> c = [c, {'end'}];
>> c = [c, {'function r = eval(self, arg)', 'r = {sin(self.d*arg{1})};'}];
>> c = [c, {'end', 'end', 'end'}];
>> d = tempname; mkdir(d); addpath(d); fid = fopen(fullfile(d, 'MyCallback.m'), 'w');
>> fprintf(fid, '%s\n', c{:}); fclose(fid);
>> f = MyCallback('f', 0.5); disp(f)
f:(i0)->(o0) CallbackInternal
>> f(2)
0.8415
>> x = MX.sym('x'); disp(f(x))
f(x){0}
>> try, jacobian(f(x), x); catch e, disp(contains(e.message, 'Derivatives cannot be')); end
1
>> f = MyCallback('f', 0.5, struct('enable_fd', true));
>> J = Function('J', {x}, {jacobian(f(x), x)}); J(2)
0.2702
>> rmpath(d); rmdir(d, 's');


julia> struct MyCallback <: ca.Callback
           d::Float64
       end
julia> ca.get_n_in(::MyCallback) = 1
julia> ca.get_n_out(::MyCallback) = 1
julia> ca.eval_(cb::MyCallback, arg) = [sin(cb.d * arg[1])]
julia> f = ca.callback(MyCallback(0.5), "f");
julia> ca.Function(f)
Function(f:(i0)->(o0) CallbackInternal)
julia> f(2)
DM(0.8415)
julia> x = ca.MX.sym("x");
julia> f(x)
MX(f(x){0})
julia> try
           ca.jacobian(f(x), x)
       catch e
           println(occursin("Derivatives cannot be calculated for f", sprint(showerror, e)))
       end
true
julia> f = ca.callback(MyCallback(0.5), "f", Dict("enable_fd" => true));
julia> J = ca.Function("J", [x], [ca.jacobian(f(x), x)]);
julia> J(2)
DM(0.2702)

The callback object must outlive every use of the Function:

>>> class Sq(Callback):
...   def __init__(self, name, opts={}):
...     Callback.__init__(self)
...     self.construct(name, opts)
...   def eval(self, arg):
...     return [arg[0]**2]
>>> x = MX.sym("x")
>>> f = Sq("f")
>>> F = Function("F", [x], [f(x)])
>>> F(3)
DM(9)
>>> del f
>>> try:
...   F(3)
... except Exception as e:
...   print(str(e).splitlines()[-1])
Callback object has been deleted


>> c = {'classdef SqCb < casadi.Callback', 'methods'};
>> c = [c, {'function self = SqCb(name)', 'self@casadi.Callback(); construct(self, name);'}];
>> c = [c, {'end'}];
>> c = [c, {'function r = eval(self, arg)', 'r = {arg{1}^2};', 'end', 'end', 'end'}];
>> d = tempname; mkdir(d); addpath(d); fid = fopen(fullfile(d, 'SqCb.m'), 'w');
>> fprintf(fid, '%s\n', c{:}); fclose(fid);
>> x = MX.sym('x'); f = SqCb('f'); F = Function('F', {x}, {f(x)}); disp(F(3))
9
>> delete(f)
>> try, F(3); catch e, disp(contains(e.message, 'Callback object has been deleted')); end
...
1
>> rmpath(d); rmdir(d, 's');


julia> struct Sq <: ca.Callback end
julia> ca.eval_(::Sq, arg) = [arg[1]^2]
julia> x = ca.MX.sym("x");
julia> f = ca.callback(Sq(), "f");
julia> F = ca.Function("F", [x], [f(x)]);
julia> F(3)
DM(9)
julia> f = nothing; GC.gc()
julia> try
           F(3)
       catch e
           println(last(split(sprint(showerror, e), "\n")))
       end
Callback object has been deleted

Use in an NLP with finite differences:

>>> class Sq(Callback):
...   def __init__(self, name, opts={}):
...     Callback.__init__(self)
...     self.construct(name, opts)
...   def eval(self, arg):
...     return [arg[0]**2]
>>> f = Sq("f", {"enable_fd": True})
>>> opti = Opti()
>>> v = opti.variable()
>>> opti.minimize(f(v-1))
>>> opti.solver("ipopt", {"print_time": False}, {"print_level": 0, "sb": "yes"})
>>> opti.solve().value(v)
1.0


>> c = {'classdef SqFd < casadi.Callback', 'methods'};
>> c = [c, {'function self = SqFd(name, opts)'}];
>> c = [c, {'self@casadi.Callback(); construct(self, name, opts);', 'end'}];
>> c = [c, {'function r = eval(self, arg)', 'r = {arg{1}^2};', 'end', 'end', 'end'}];
>> d = tempname; mkdir(d); addpath(d); fid = fopen(fullfile(d, 'SqFd.m'), 'w');
>> fprintf(fid, '%s\n', c{:}); fclose(fid);
>> f = SqFd('f', struct('enable_fd', true));
>> opti = Opti(); v = opti.variable(); opti.minimize(f(v-1));
>> opti.solver('ipopt', struct('print_time', false), struct('print_level', 0, 'sb', 'yes'));
>> sol = opti.solve(); disp(sol.value(v))
1.0000
>> rmpath(d); rmdir(d, 's');


julia> struct Sq <: ca.Callback end
julia> ca.eval_(::Sq, arg) = [arg[1]^2]
julia> f = ca.callback(Sq(), "f", Dict("enable_fd" => true));
julia> opti = ca.Opti();
julia> v = ca.variable(opti);
julia> ca.minimize(opti, f(v - 1))
julia> ca.solver(opti, "ipopt", Dict("print_time" => false),
                  Dict("print_level" => 0, "sb" => "yes"))
julia> ca.value(ca.solve(opti), v)
1.0

arg is a flat activity mask over all input nonzeros (size nnz_in(), true = active = possibly nonzero); the result is the corresponding mask over all output nonzeros (size nnz_out()). An output that comes out inactive (false) is guaranteed zero for any value of the active inputs. Unlike sparsity propagation this exploits annihilation: an inactive operand of a multiply kills the product.

Function casadi::Function::bspline ( const std::string &  name,
const std::vector< std::vector< double > > &  knots,
const std::vector< double > &  coeffs,

casadi_int  m = 1,
const Dict &  opts = Dict() 
)
staticinherited

The result maps a point of dimension len(knots) (one column vector input) to the m-dimensional spline value. Coefficients are stored flat in coeffs with the value dimension m fastest, then the first spline dimension, etc.; the number of coefficients per dimension is len(knots[d]) - degree[d] - 1. A mismatch between the lengths of knots and degree raises an error. For data-driven splines or general interpolation see interpolant.

Parameters
nameName of the result
knotsKnot vector per dimension, non-decreasing, with repeated end knots
coeffsFlat coefficient list
degreePolynomial degree per dimension
mDimension of the spline value
opts"lookup_mode" (per dimension: "linear", "exact", "binary") and Function options

>>> f = Function.bspline("f", [[0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 2, 2]], [0, 1, 2, 3], [2])
>>> f
Function(f:(i0)->(o0) MXFunction)
>>> f(0), f(0.5), f(2)
(DM(0), DM(0.875), DM(3))
>>> g = Function.bspline("g", [[0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 1, 1]], [0, 1, 2, 3], [1, 1])
>>> g([0.5, 0.5])
DM(1.5)
>>> try:
...   Function.bspline("f", [[0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 2, 2]], [0, 1, 2, 3], [2, 2])
... except RuntimeError as e:
...   print("must match knot list length" in str(e))
True


>> knots = {[0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 2, 2]};
>> f = Function.bspline('f', knots, [0, 1, 2, 3], 2); disp(f)

◆ cache()

Dict casadi::Function::cache ( ) const
inherited

jacobian, forward, reverse, wrap and serial map store their result in a cache keyed by name (jac_f, fwd1_f, adj1_f, wrap_f, map3_f, ...). The cache holds weak references: an entry stays only while some other reference keeps the function alive. Option "cache" prepopulates it, e.g. with a hand-written Jacobian.

>>> x = SX.sym("x")
>>> f = Function("f", [x], [sin(x)])
>>> f.cache()
{}
>>> J = f.jacobian()
>>> list(f.cache().keys())
['jac_f']


>> x = SX.sym('x');
>> f = Function('f', {x}, {sin(x)});
>> isempty(fieldnames(f.cache()))
1
>> J = f.jacobian(); disp(strjoin(fieldnames(f.cache()), ' '))
jac_f

◆ call() [1/6]

void casadi::Function::call ( const DMDict &  arg,
DMDict &  res,
bool  always_inline = false,
bool  never_inline = false 
) const
inherited

This is the general evaluation entry point; the call operator (f(...) in Python, C++ and MATLAB) is a shorthand for it. Argument lists must have exactly n_in() entries. A dict maps input names to values; missing inputs take default_in, unknown names raise an error. The result is a list of n_out() values, or a dict keyed by output name.

The argument type selects the evaluation mode:

  • DM (or anything convertible to DM, such as numbers and numeric arrays): numerical evaluation, returns DM
  • SX: symbolic evaluation producing an SX expression; an MX function is expanded on the fly (fails if it contains non-expandable nodes)
  • MX: symbolic evaluation producing a call node f(args){k} in the MX graph, unless the function is inlined

Shapes: each argument must have the input shape, or be a scalar (broadcast to all entries), a transposed vector, an empty matrix (treated as all zeros), or N-by-(P*M) for an N-by-M input (P evaluations, outputs stacked horizontally; other arguments are repeated). Anything else raises an error that lists these rules. Sparsity is projected: entries outside sparsity_in are ignored. When all inputs are scalar and the arguments are matrices of one common shape, the function is applied elementwise. Numerical evaluation of a function with free variables raises "Cannot evaluate ... since variables [...] are free".

Parameters
argList or dict of arguments, all of the same type
resOutput: list or dict of results
always_inlineMX only: expand the call into the caller's graph instead of creating a call node (SX functions are then inlined as scalar operations); combined with never_inline raises an error
never_inlineSX only: keep the call as an opaque call node inside the SX expression instead of inlining it

>>> x = SX.sym("x"); y = SX.sym("y", 2)
>>> f = Function("f", [x, y], [x*y, sin(x)], ["x", "y"], ["r", "s"])
>>> f.call([2, [3, 4]])
[DM([6, 8]), DM(0.909297)]
>>> f.call({"x": 2})
{'r': DM([0, 0]), 's': DM(0.909297)}
>>> f(2, [3, 4])
(DM([6, 8]), DM(0.909297))
>>> f(x=2, y=[3, 4])
{'r': DM([6, 8]), 's': DM(0.909297)}
>>> f(2, DM([[3, 5], [4, 6]]))
(DM(
[[6, 10],
 [8, 12]]), DM([[0.909297, 0.909297]]))
>>> f(DM(0, 0), 3)
(DM([0, 0]), DM(0))
>>> z = MX.sym("z"); w = MX.sym("w", 2)
>>> f.call([z, w])
[MX(f(z, w){0}), MX(f(z, w){1})]
>>> f.call([z, w], True)
[MX(vertcat((z*w[0]), (z*w[1]))), MX(sin(z))]
>>> a = SX.sym("a")
>>> f.call([a, [1, 2]])
[SX([a, (2.*a)]), SX(sin(a))]
>>> try:
...   f(1)
... except RuntimeError as e:
...   print("Incorrect number of inputs: Expected 2, got 1" in str(e))
True
>>> try:
...   f(1, [1, 2, 3])
... except RuntimeError as e:
...   print("Input 1 (y) has mismatching shape. Got 3-by-1" in str(e))
True


>> x = SX.sym('x'); y = SX.sym('y', 2);
>> f = Function('f', {x, y}, {x*y, sin(x)}, {'x', 'y'}, {'r', 's'});
>> res = f.call({2, [3; 4]}); disp(res{1}), disp(res{2})

◆ call() [2/6]

void casadi::Function::call ( const MXDict &  arg,
MXDict &  res,
bool  always_inline = false,
bool  never_inline = false

inherited

This is the general evaluation entry point; the call operator (f(...) in Python, C++ and MATLAB) is a shorthand for it. Argument lists must have exactly n_in() entries. A dict maps input names to values; missing inputs take default_in, unknown names raise an error. The result is a list of n_out() values, or a dict keyed by output name.

The argument type selects the evaluation mode:

  • DM (or anything convertible to DM, such as numbers and numeric arrays): numerical evaluation, returns DM
  • SX: symbolic evaluation producing an SX expression; an MX function is expanded on the fly (fails if it contains non-expandable nodes)
  • MX: symbolic evaluation producing a call node f(args){k} in the MX graph, unless the function is inlined

Shapes: each argument must have the input shape, or be a scalar (broadcast to all entries), a transposed vector, an empty matrix (treated as all zeros), or N-by-(P*M) for an N-by-M input (P evaluations, outputs stacked horizontally; other arguments are repeated). Anything else raises an error that lists these rules. Sparsity is projected: entries outside sparsity_in are ignored. When all inputs are scalar and the arguments are matrices of one common shape, the function is applied elementwise. Numerical evaluation of a function with free variables raises "Cannot evaluate ... since variables [...] are free".

Parameters
argList or dict of arguments, all of the same type
resOutput: list or dict of results
always_inlineMX only: expand the call into the caller's graph instead of creating a call node (SX functions are then inlined as scalar operations); combined with never_inline raises an error
never_inlineSX only: keep the call as an opaque call node inside the SX expression instead of inlining it

>>> f = Function("f", [x, y], [x*y, sin(x)], ["x", "y"], ["r", "s"])
>>> f.call([2, [3, 4]])
[DM([6, 8]), DM(0.909297)]
>>> f.call({"x": 2})
{'r': DM([0, 0]), 's': DM(0.909297)}
>>> f(2, [3, 4])
(DM([6, 8]), DM(0.909297))
>>> f(x=2, y=[3, 4])
{'r': DM([6, 8]), 's': DM(0.909297)}
>>> f(2, DM([[3, 5], [4, 6]]))
(DM(
[[6, 10],

>>> f(DM(0, 0), 3)

>>> z = MX.sym("z"); w = MX.sym("w", 2)

>>> f.call([z, w], True)
[MX(vertcat((z*w[0]), (z*w[1]))), MX(sin(z))]
>>> a = SX.sym("a")

True

◆ call() [5/6]

void casadi::Function::call ( const std::vector< SX > &  arg,
std::vector< SX > &  res,
bool  always_inline = false,
bool  never_inline = false 
) const
inherited

This is the general evaluation entry point; the call operator (f(...) in Python, C++ and MATLAB) is a shorthand for it. Argument lists must have exactly n_in() entries. A dict maps input names to values; missing inputs take default_in, unknown names raise an error. The result is a list of n_out() values, or a dict keyed by output name.

The argument type selects the evaluation mode:

  • DM (or anything convertible to DM, such as numbers and numeric arrays): numerical evaluation, returns DM
  • SX: symbolic evaluation producing an SX expression; an MX function is expanded on the fly (fails if it contains non-expandable nodes)
  • MX: symbolic evaluation producing a call node f(args){k} in the MX graph, unless the function is inlined

Shapes: each argument must have the input shape, or be a scalar (broadcast to all entries), a transposed vector, an empty matrix (treated as all zeros), or N-by-(P*M) for an N-by-M input (P evaluations, outputs stacked horizontally; other arguments are repeated). Anything else raises an error that lists these rules. Sparsity is projected: entries outside sparsity_in are ignored. When all inputs are scalar and the arguments are matrices of one common shape, the function is applied elementwise. Numerical evaluation of a function with free variables raises "Cannot evaluate ... since variables [...] are free".

Parameters
argList or dict of arguments, all of the same type
resOutput: list or dict of results
always_inlineMX only: expand the call into the caller's graph instead of creating a call node (SX functions are then inlined as scalar operations); combined with never_inline raises an error
never_inlineSX only: keep the call as an opaque call node inside the SX expression instead of inlining it

[DM([6, 8]), DM(0.909297)]

◆ check_name()

bool casadi::Function::check_name ( const std::string &  name)
staticinherited

A valid name starts with a letter and continues with letters, digits and underscores, with no two consecutive underscores; it may not be one of the keywords "null", "jac", "hess". Constructors and generate raise for invalid names; names must be valid C identifiers because they appear in generated code.

>>> Function.check_name("f_1"), Function.check_name("1f")
(True, False)
>>> Function.check_name("a__b"), Function.check_name("jac"), Function.check_name("")
(False, False, False)

◆ checkout()

casadi_int casadi::Function::checkout ( ) const
inherited

Each memory object holds the state of one evaluation context (solver workspace, statistics); ordinary calls use index 0. Reserving separate objects allows concurrent evaluation from several threads with the low-level interface and separate stats. Release it with release when done.

1

◆ conditional() [2/2]

Function casadi::Function::conditional ( const std::string &  name,
const std::vector< Function > &  f,
const Function &  f_def,
const Dict &  opts = Dict() 
)
staticinherited

The result takes an index as first input followed by the inputs of the branch functions. At evaluation the index is truncated to an integer k; branch f[k] is evaluated when 0 <= k < len(f), otherwise f_def. All branches must have the same number of inputs and outputs; the signature (names, shapes) is taken from f_def and arguments are projected when a branch has a different sparsity. Derivatives are the derivatives of the selected branch. Symbolic MX evaluation gives a call node; unlike if_else on expressions, only the selected branch is evaluated numerically.

Parameters
nameName of the result
fBranch functions, selected by index 0, 1, ...
f_defDefault branch for indices out of range
optsFunction options

>>> x = SX.sym("x")
>>> f0 = Function("f0", [x], [x]); f1 = Function("f1", [x], [x**2])
>>> fdef = Function("fdef", [x], [-x])
>>> sw = Function.conditional("sw", [f0, f1], fdef)
>>> sw
Function(sw:(i0,i1)->(o0) Switch)
>>> sw(0, 3), sw(1, 3), sw(1.9, 3), sw(2, 3), sw(-1, 3)
(DM(3), DM(9), DM(9), DM(-3), DM(-3))
>>> sw(MX.sym("k"), MX.sym("v"))
MX(sw(k, v){0})

◆ construct() [1/4]

void casadi::Callback::construct ( const std::string &  name,
const Dict &  opts = Dict() 
)

The class constructor only creates a null pointer; this call creates the Function. It must be called once from the subclass constructor, after all data needed by get_n_in/get_n_out/get_sparsity_in/get_sparsity_out/get_name_in/get_name_out is set, because those methods are evaluated here. init() and finalize() are called at the end. Calling it twice raises an error.

Parameters
nameName of the Function
optsFunction options, e.g. "enable_fd", "fd_method", "fd_options", "enable_forward", "enable_reverse", "enable_jacobian"

>>> class Sq(Callback):
...   def __init__(self, name, opts={}):
...     Callback.__init__(self)
...     self.construct(name, opts)
...   def eval(self, arg):
...     return [arg[0]**2]
>>> f = Sq("f", {"enable_fd": True, "fd_method": "forward"})
>>> f.name(), f.n_in(), f.n_out()
('f', 1, 1)
>>> try:
...   f.construct("g")
... except Exception as e:
...   print("Internal class already created" in str(e))
True

◆ convert_in() [1/6]

std::vector< DM > casadi::Function::convert_in ( const DMDict &  arg) const
inherited

convert_in turns a list of n_in() values into a dict keyed by input name, and a dict into a list where absent inputs get default_in. convert_out does the same for outputs; absent outputs become nan. An unknown key or a list of the wrong length raises an error. Values are passed through unchanged (no shape or sparsity check), for any of DM, SX and MX. Useful to prepare arguments for call or generate_in.

>>> f = Function("f", [SX.sym("x"), SX.sym("y")], [SX(0), SX(1)], ["x", "y"], ["a", "b"])
>>> f.convert_in([1, 2])
{'x': DM(1), 'y': DM(2)}
>>> f.convert_in({"y": 2})
[DM(0), DM(2)]
>>> f.convert_out({"b": 5})
[DM(nan), DM(5)]
>>> try:
...   f.convert_in({"z": 1})
... except RuntimeError as e:
...   print('could not find entry "z"' in str(e))
True


>> f = Function('f', {SX.sym('x'), SX.sym('y')}, {SX(0), SX(1)}, {'x', 'y'}, {'a', 'b'});
>> s = f.convert_in({1, 2}); disp(s.x), disp(s.y)
1
2
>> c = f.convert_in(struct('y', 2)); disp(c{1}), disp(c{2})
0
2
>> c = f.convert_out(struct('b', 5)); disp(c{1}), disp(c{2})
nan
5
>> try, f.convert_in(struct('z', 1)); catch e, msg = e.message; end
>> contains(msg, 'could not find entry "z"')
1

◆ default_in()

double casadi::Function::default_in ( casadi_int  ind) const
inherited

When calling with a dict (or keyword arguments), every input that is not given is filled with this scalar, broadcast to the input shape. For functions built from expressions it is 0 unless option "default_in" was set at construction. Solvers define their own: nlpsol uses -inf for lbx and lbg, inf for ubx and ubg, 0 for the rest.

>>> x = SX.sym("x"); y = SX.sym("y", 2)
>>> f = Function("f", [x, y], [x + y], ["x", "y"], ["r"])
>>> f.default_in(0), f(x=3)
(0.0, {'r': DM([3, 3])})
>>> g = Function("g", [x, y], [x + y], ["x", "y"], ["r"], {"default_in": [1, 2]})
>>> g.default_in(1), g(x=3), g(y=[0, 1])
(2.0, {'r': DM([5, 5])}, {'r': DM([1, 2])})


>> x = SX.sym('x'); y = SX.sym('y', 2);
>> f = Function('f', {x, y}, {x + y}, {'x', 'y'}, {'r'});
>> disp(f.default_in(0)), res = f('x', 3); disp(res.r)
0
[3, 3]
>> opts = struct('default_in', [1, 2]);
>> g = Function('g', {x, y}, {x + y}, {'x', 'y'}, {'r'}, opts);
>> disp(g.default_in(1)), res = g('x', 3); disp(res.r), res = g('y', [0; 1]); disp(res.r)
2
[5, 5]
[1, 2]


julia> x = ca.SX.sym("x"); y = ca.SX.sym("y", 2);
julia> f = ca.Function("f", [x, y], [x + y], ["x", "y"], ["r"]);
julia> ca.default_in(f, 0), f(x=3)["r"]
(0.0, [3, 3])
julia> opts = Dict("default_in" => [1, 2]);

◆ eval()

std::vector< DM > casadi::Callback::eval ( const std::vector< DM > &  arg) const
virtual

The method a subclass must implement. Receives one DM per input (with the sparsity of get_sparsity_in) and must return a list with one entry per output; each entry is converted to a DM and must match the shape of get_sparsity_out, otherwise the call raises an error. Exceptions raised inside propagate to the caller. The default implementation raises an error.

This signature is not thread-safe. For guaranteed thread-safety, use eval_buffer.

Parameters
argInput values
Returns
Output values

>>> class Scale(Callback):
...   def __init__(self, name, opts={}):
...     Callback.__init__(self)
...     self.construct(name, opts)
...   def get_n_in(self): return 2
...   def get_sparsity_in(self, i):
...     return Sparsity.dense(2, 1) if i == 0 else Sparsity.dense(1, 1)
...   def get_sparsity_out(self, i): return Sparsity.dense(2, 1)
...   def eval(self, arg):
...     return [arg[0]*arg[1]]
>>> f = Scale("f")
>>> f([1, 2], 3)
DM([3, 6])
>>> class Bad(Scale):
...   def eval(self, arg):
...     return [arg[1]]
>>> try:
...   Bad("b")([1, 2], 3)
... except Exception as e:
...   print("Shape mismatch" in str(e))
True

◆ eval_buffer()

int casadi::Callback::eval_buffer ( const double **  arg,
const std::vector< casadi_int > &  sizes_arg,
double **  res,
const std::vector< casadi_int > &  sizes_res 
) const
virtual

Alternative to eval() that works on the raw nonzero buffers, avoiding DM allocation. Override has_eval_buffer() to return true to activate it. In Python the method receives two tuples of memoryview objects (inputs and outputs), each holding only the structural nonzeros of the corresponding input or output in column-major order; write the result into the output buffers and return 0.

>>> class Sq(Callback):
...   def __init__(self, name, opts={}):
...     Callback.__init__(self)
...     self.construct(name, opts)
...   def get_sparsity_in(self, i): return Sparsity.dense(3, 1)
...   def get_sparsity_out(self, i): return Sparsity.dense(3, 1)
...   def has_eval_buffer(self): return True
...   def eval_buffer(self, arg, res):
...     a = np.frombuffer(arg[0], dtype=np.float64)
...     r = np.frombuffer(res[0], dtype=np.float64)
...     r[:] = a**2
...     return 0
>>> f = Sq("f")
>>> f([1, 2, 3])
DM([1, 4, 9])


julia> struct Sq <: ca.Callback end
julia> ca.get_sparsity_in(::Sq, i) = ca.Sparsity.dense(3, 1)
julia> ca.get_sparsity_out(::Sq, i) = ca.Sparsity.dense(3, 1)
julia> ca.has_eval_buffer(::Sq) = true
julia> ca.eval_buffer(::Sq, arg, res) = (res[1] .= arg[1] .^ 2; 0)
julia> f = ca.callback(Sq(), "f");
julia> f([1, 2, 3])
DM([1, 4, 9])

◆ expand() [1/2]

Function casadi::Function::expand ( ) const
inherited

Evaluates the function symbolically with SX inputs and builds an SXFunction from the result: every matrix node is unrolled into scalar instructions. Evaluation of the result is typically faster per operation, at the cost of memory proportional to the number of scalar operations. The name, input/output names and the options of the original function (other than the SX-specific ones given in opts) are kept.

Fails when the graph contains a node that has no scalar expansion, with "eval_sx not defined for ...": for example calls to external functions or linear solves (solve, inv) with a numerical plugin; use the "symbolicqr" plugin for those. Fails when the function has free variables. An SXFunction is returned unchanged (as a copy).

Parameters
nameName of the new function; defaults to the current name
optsOptions for the SXFunction constructor, e.g. "live_variables", "cse"
Returns
SXFunction

>>> x = MX.sym("x", 2)
>>> f = Function("f", [x], [x.T @ x, 2*x], ["x"], ["q", "y"])
>>> f, f.n_instructions()
(Function(f:(x[2])->(q,y[2]) MXFunction), 7)
>>> g = f.expand()
>>> g, g.n_instructions()
(Function(f:(x[2])->(q,y[2]) SXFunction), 10)
>>> f([1, 2]), g([1, 2])
((DM(5), DM([2, 4])), (DM(5), DM([2, 4])))
>>> f.expand("f_sx", {"live_variables": False})
Function(f_sx:(x[2])->(q,y[2]) SXFunction)
>>> A = MX.sym("A", 2, 2)
>>> h = Function("h", [A, x], [solve(A, x)])
>>> try:
...   h.expand()
... except RuntimeError as e:
...   print("eval_sx not defined" in str(e))
True
>>> Function("h", [A, x], [solve(A, x, "symbolicqr")]).expand().class_name()
'SXFunction'


>> x = MX.sym('x', 2);
>> f = Function('f', {x}, {x'*x, 2*x}, {'x'}, {'q', 'y'});
>> f, f.n_instructions()
f:(x[2])->(q,y[2]) MXFunction
7
>> g = f.expand(); disp(g), disp(g.n_instructions())
f:(x[2])->(q,y[2]) SXFunction
10
>> [q, y] = g([1; 2]); disp(q), disp(y)
5
[2, 4]
>> f.expand('f_sx', struct('live_variables', false))
f_sx:(x[2])->(q,y[2]) SXFunction
>> A = MX.sym('A', 2, 2); h = Function('h', {A, x}, {solve(A, x)});
>> try, h.expand(); catch e, disp(contains(e.message, 'eval_sx not defined')); end

HTML and .casadi_viz embed the serialized Function, decoded by the browser viewer; any serializable Function works, and helpers such as nlp_hess_l can be explored. include_functions (default true) shows called and helper Functions in the viewer. DOT is standalone Graphviz of an SX/MX root graph only. Options show_matrix_contents and show_matrix_sizes (both default true) control matrix detail and dimensions. Load dump_trace JSONL files in the viewer to replay numerical evaluation. Options: view (function, expression; default function), direction (LR, RL, TB, BT; expression view only; default TB), viz_js (local Viz.js global bundle to embed; by default uses the viewer package renderer). viewer_url (string) overrides the HTML viewer ESM module URL; default is https://unpkg.com/@casadi/casadi-viz@MAJOR.MINOR/dist/index.js for this CasADi version.

◆ factory()

Function casadi::Function::factory ( const std::string &  name,
const std::vector< std::string > &  s_in,
const std::vector< std::string > &  s_out,
const AuxOut &  aux = AuxOut(),
const Dict &  opts = Dict() 
) const
inherited

Only defined for SXFunction and MXFunction (other classes raise an error). The new function takes the inputs listed in s_in and returns the outputs listed in s_out, in that order. Each entry is either an existing name or a derivative request built from existing names with ':' separators:

  • inputs: "fwd:x" a forward seed for input x, "adj:r" an adjoint seed for output r, "lam:r" a multiplier for output r (used by aux)
  • outputs: "fwd:r" forward sensitivity, "adj:x" adjoint sensitivity, "jac:r:x" the Jacobian of r with respect to x, "grad:r:x" its gradient (r must be scalar), "hess:r:x:y" the Hessian of scalar r with respect to x and y
  • an output may be prefixed with "triu:", "tril:" or "sym:" to return only the upper or lower triangle of a Hessian, or to symmetrize it

The output names of the result have ':' replaced by '_' (jac:r:x becomes jac_r_x). Non-differentiable inputs and outputs (is_diff_in/is_diff_out) give all-zero blocks. An input that is needed by an output but not listed in s_in is treated as zero. An unknown name raises an error listing the available names.

Parameters
nameName of the new function
s_inInput requests, see above
s_outOutput requests, see above
auxExtra scalar outputs defined as linear combinations: {"gamma": ["f", "g"]} defines gamma = lam_f'*f + lam_g'*g, so that "grad:gamma:x" and "hess:gamma:x:x" are the Lagrangian gradient and Hessian with inputs "lam:f" and "lam:g"
opts"helper_options" and "final_options" (dicts for the intermediate and the returned function) and any Function option for the result

◆ fold()

Function casadi::Function::fold ( casadi_int  N,
const Dict &  opts = Dict() 
) const
inherited

as inputs

The first n_accum inputs are accumulators: in every step they take the value of the first n_accum outputs of the previous step. For a step f:(x, u)->(x_next, y) the result is F:(x0, U)->(X, Y) with U = horzcat(u0, ..., u_(N-1)), X = horzcat(x1, ..., x_N), Y = horzcat(y0, ..., y_(N-1)) and x_(k+1), y_k = f(x_k, u_k). Non-accumulated inputs and all outputs are stacked horizontally over the N steps; the accumulator inputs keep their original shape. An accumulator output may be wider than its input (e.g. 1-by-2 feeding a 1-by-1 input): only the last columns are fed back.

Compared with writing the loop in the host language the construction is much faster and the graph is a tower of nested unrolled loops of at most base iterations (option "base", default 10; -1 unrolls completely). This keeps memory use proportional to base rather than N at a small evaluation cost.

The overloads differ in how accumulators are selected: a count n_accum (default 1), or explicit index/name lists accum_in and accum_out of equal length that may pick arbitrary inputs and outputs. The unnamed overload names the result "mapaccum_" + name(). fold is mapaccum returning only the final accumulator state.

Parameters
nameName of the result
NNumber of steps, must be positive
n_accumNumber of leading inputs/outputs that are accumulated; at most min(n_in, n_out)
opts"base" plus options for the resulting MXFunction

>>> step = Function("step", [x, u], [x + u, x*u], ["x", "u"], ["x_next", "y"])

◆ forward()

The result is named fwd<nfwd>_<name> and has n_in + n_out + n_in inputs: the original inputs, the original outputs (out_<name>, read only when uses_output() is true) and the forward seeds fwd_<input>, each with nfwd times the columns of the input. Uses the class' own forward mode when available ("enable_forward"), finite differences when "enable_fd" is set, or otherwise the full Jacobian; raises "Derivatives cannot be calculated" when none applies. Results are cached while alive. nfwd must be positive.

◆ generate() [2/2]

std::string casadi::Function::generate ( const std::string &  fname,
const Dict &  opts = Dict() 
) const
inherited

Writes fname (a ".c" suffix is added when missing; the base name must satisfy check_name) in the current directory and returns the file name. The generated file exports, for a function named f, the evaluation routine int f(const casadi_real** arg, casadi_real** res, casadi_int* iw, casadi_real* w, int mem) plus f_n_in, f_n_out, f_name_in, f_name_out, f_sparsity_in, f_sparsity_out, f_work, f_checkout, f_release, f_incref, f_decref and f_default_in. The arrays hold the nonzeros of each input and output in column-major order; work vector sizes come from f_work. Functions embedded in the graph (solvers, maps, ...) are generated too when they support code generation; otherwise an error is raised. The same file can hold several functions via the CodeGenerator class.

Parameters
fnameFile name, e.g. "f.c" or "f"
optsCode generator options: "with_header" (also write a .h file), "main" (add a main() reading inputs from a file written by generate_in), "casadi_real" (scalar type, default "double"), "casadi_int" (integer type), "with_mem" (simplified memory API), "mex", "cpp", "indent", "prefix", "verbose", "with_export", "with_import", "include_math", "infinity", "nan", "real_min", "unroll_args", "codegen_scalars", "avoid_stack", "thread_safe", "force_canonical"

>>> import os
>>> x = SX.sym("x"); y = SX.sym("y", 2)
>>> f = Function("f", [x, y], [x*y, sin(x)], ["x", "y"], ["r", "s"])
>>> fname = f.generate("f.c")
>>> fname, os.path.isfile("f.c")
('f.c', True)
>>> src = open("f.c").read()
>>> print("int f(const casadi_real** arg, casadi_real** res" in src, "f_n_in" in src)
True True
>>> os.remove("f.c")
>>> f.generate("g", {"with_header": True}), sorted(os.listdir(".")).count("g.h")
('g.c', 1)
>>> os.remove("g.c"); os.remove("g.h")


>> x = SX.sym('x'); y = SX.sym('y', 2);

std::vector< DM > casadi::Function::generate_in ( const std::string &  fname)

With arguments, writes the nonzeros of arg (one value per line, in input order) to fname; this is the input format read by code generated with option "main". Without arguments, reads such a file back into a list of DM with the input sparsities. The arguments follow the shape rules of call (scalars are broadcast); a file with the wrong number of values raises a dimension error.

Function casadi::Callback::get_forward ( casadi_int  nfwd,

) const
virtual

Override has_forward(nfwd) to return true for the numbers of directions you support (nfwd==1 is enough; CasADi then loops) and get_forward() to return a Function with inputs [nominal inputs, nominal outputs, one forward seed per input] and one forward sensitivity per output. For nfwd>1 the seeds and sensitivities are horizontally stacked (n-by-nfwd*m). forward(nfwd) on the Function caches the result.

>>> class Sq(Callback):
...   def __init__(self, name, opts={}):
...     Callback.__init__(self)
...     self.construct(name, opts)
...   def eval(self, arg):
...     return [arg[0]**2]
...   def has_forward(self, nfwd): return nfwd == 1
...   def get_forward(self, nfwd, name, inames, onames, opts):
...     print(nfwd, name, inames, onames)
...     x, y, xd = SX.sym("x"), SX.sym("y", Sparsity(1, 1)), SX.sym("xd")
...     return Function(name, [x, y, xd], [2*x*xd], inames, onames, opts)
>>> f = Sq("f")
>>> x = MX.sym("x")
>>> J = Function("J", [x], [jacobian(f(x), x)])
1 fwd1_f ['i0', 'out_o0', 'fwd_i0'] ['fwd_o0']
>>> J(3)
DM(6)

◆ get_function() [1/2]

std::vector< std::string > casadi::Function::get_function ( ) const
inherited

For an SXFunction or MXFunction: the functions called in its graph (an MXFunction called with MX arguments is inlined and does not appear; SX functions, solvers and calls made with never_inline do); for a map: the mapped function; for a solver: its helper functions (e.g. nlp_f, nlp_jac_g for nlpsol, which can also be code-generated with generate_dependencies). Empty for leaf classes. Note that has_function only answers true for solver objects; for SX and MX functions it is false even for names in this list.

inlinevirtual

with respect to all output elements. Override has_jac_sparsity(oind, iind) to return true and get_jac_sparsity() to return the pattern of the Jacobian block of output oind with respect to input iind. Without it the block is assumed dense. Finite differencing exploits the pattern (fewer evaluations) and the result of jacobian() carries it.

...   def get_sparsity_out(self, i): return Sparsity.dense(3, 1)

...     return [arg[0]**2]
...   def has_jac_sparsity(self, oind, iind): return True
...   def get_jac_sparsity(self, oind, iind, symmetric): return Sparsity.diag(3)

◆ get_jacobian()

Function casadi::Callback::get_jacobian ( const std::string &  name,
const std::vector< std::string > &  inames,
const std::vector< std::string > &  onames,
const Dict &  opts 
) const
virtual

Override has_jacobian() to return true and get_jacobian() to return a Function with inputs [all nominal inputs, all nominal outputs] and one output per (output, input) pair, each the dense or sparse Jacobian block of that output with respect to that input (row-major over the pairs). Use the inames, onames and opts passed in: they carry the expected names and the "derivative_of" option. The returned Function may be an SX/MX Function (then higher derivatives are exact) or another Callback (keep a reference to it).

>>> class F43(Callback):
...   def __init__(self, name, opts={}):
...     Callback.__init__(self)
...     self.construct(name, opts)
...   def get_sparsity_in(self, i): return Sparsity.dense(4, 1)
...   def get_sparsity_out(self, i): return Sparsity.dense(3, 1)
...   def eval(self, arg):
...     a, b, c, d = vertsplit(arg[0])
...     return [vertcat(sin(c)*d+d**2, 2*a+c, b**2+5*c)]
...   def has_jacobian(self): return True
...   def get_jacobian(self, name, inames, onames, opts):
...     print(name, inames, onames)
...     x = SX.sym("x", 4)
...     y = SX.sym("y", Sparsity(3, 1))
...     a, b, c, d = vertsplit(x)
...     J = blockcat([[0, 0, d*cos(c), sin(c)+2*d], [2, 0, 1, 0], [0, 2*b, 5, 0]])
...     return Function(name, [x, y], [J], inames, onames, opts)
>>> f = F43("f")
>>> x = MX.sym("x", 4)
>>> J = Function("J", [x], [jacobian(f(x), x)])
jac_f ['i0', 'out_o0'] ['jac_o0_i0']
>>> J([1, 2, 0, 3])
DM(
[[0, 0, 3, 6],
 [2, 0, 1, 0],
 [0, 4, 5, 0]])

Override has_reverse(nadj) to return true for the numbers of directions you support and get_reverse() to return a Function with inputs [nominal inputs, nominal outputs, one adjoint seed per output] and one adjoint sensitivity per input. For nadj>1 the seeds and sensitivities are horizontally stacked. Reverse mode is what gradient-based NLP solvers use for the objective gradient. reverse(nadj) caches the result.

>>> class Sq(Callback):

...   def has_reverse(self, nadj): return nadj == 1
...   def get_reverse(self, nadj, name, inames, onames, opts):
...     print(nadj, name, inames, onames)
...     x, y, yb = SX.sym("x"), SX.sym("y", Sparsity(1, 1)), SX.sym("yb")
...     return Function(name, [x, y, yb], [2*x*yb], inames, onames, opts)

For nadj>1 the seeds and sensitivities are horizontally stacked. Reverse mode is what gradient-based NLP solvers use for the objective gradient. reverse(nadj) caches the result.

>>> class Sq(Callback):
...   def __init__(self, name, opts={}):
...     Callback.__init__(self)
...     self.construct(name, opts)
...   def eval(self, arg):
...     return [arg[0]**2]
...   def has_reverse(self, nadj): return nadj == 1
...   def get_reverse(self, nadj, name, inames, onames, opts):
...     print(nadj, name, inames, onames)
...     x, y, yb = SX.sym("x"), SX.sym("y", Sparsity(1, 1)), SX.sym("yb")
...     return Function(name, [x, y, yb], [2*x*yb], inames, onames, opts)
>>> f = Sq("f")
>>> x = MX.sym("x")
>>> G = Function("G", [x], [gradient(f(x), x)])
1 adj1_f ['i0', 'out_o0', 'adj_o0'] ['adj_i0']
>>> G(3)
DM(6)

>> c = [c, {'function self = SqAdj(name)'}];
>> c = [c, {'self@casadi.Callback(); construct(self, name);', 'end'}];
>> c = [c, {'function r = eval(self, arg)', 'r = {arg{1}^2};', 'end'}];
>> c = [c, {'function b = has_reverse(self, nadj)', 'b = nadj == 1;', 'end'}];
>> c = [c, {'function F = get_reverse(self, nadj, name, inames, onames, opts)'}];
>> c = [c, {'disp(nadj); disp(name); disp(inames); disp(onames);'}];

◆ jacobian()

Function casadi::Function::jacobian ( ) const
inherited

The result is named jac_<name> and takes all inputs followed by all outputs (named out_<output>); the output values are only read when uses_output() is true and may be passed as 0 otherwise. It returns one block per (output, input) pair, ordered by output first: for f:(x,y)->(r,s) the outputs are jac_r_x, jac_r_y, jac_s_x, jac_s_y. Blocks involving a non-differentiable input or output are all-zero sparse. Each block is a size_out(o)-times-size_in(i) matrix where the output and input are vectorized column-major; blocks that are structurally zero have an all-zero sparsity pattern.

The result is cached: calling jacobian again returns the same object as long as it is alive. The derivative itself is built by symbolic AD for SX and MX functions, by the solver's own sensitivity method for solver objects, or raises "Derivatives cannot be calculated" for classes without any derivative support. For a single block, factory("...", ..., ["jac:r:x"]) avoids computing the others.

>>> x = SX.sym("x"); y = SX.sym("y", 2)
>>> f = Function("f", [x, y], [x*y, sin(x)], ["x", "y"], ["r", "s"])
>>> J = f.jacobian()
>>> print(J)
jac_f:(x,y[2],out_r[2x1,0nz],out_s[1x1,0nz])->(jac_r_x[2],jac_r_y[2x2,2nz],...) SXFunction
>>> J(1, [2, 3], 0, 0)
(DM([2, 3]), DM(
[[1, 00],
 [00, 1]]), DM(0.540302), DM([[00, 00]]))
>>> f.jacobian().name_out()
['jac_r_x', 'jac_r_y', 'jac_s_x', 'jac_s_y']

◆ jit() [1/2]

Function casadi::Function::jit ( const std::string &  name,
const std::string &  body,
const std::vector< std::string > &  name_in,
const std::vector< std::string > &  name_out,
const Dict &  opts = Dict() 
)
staticinherited

body is the body of a C function that is compiled with the "compiler" plugin (option "compiler", default "shell" i.e. the system C compiler on most builds, or "clang") and loaded as an external function. This needs a working C compiler at run time; the source and library files are removed afterwards unless "jit_cleanup" is false.

Inside the body, the nonzeros of input k are available through a pointer named name_in[k] (type const casadi_real*) and the nonzeros of output k must be written through a pointer named name_out[k] (type casadi_real*), in column-major order of the sparsity pattern. casadi_real is double unless the code generator is told otherwise. By default (option "buffered": true) inputs and outputs are copied through a work vector, so the pointers are never null; with "buffered": false a null input means all-zero and a null output may be skipped. Write "return 1;" to signal an evaluation failure.

The result has no derivatives unless option "enable_fd": true (finite differences) is passed or a C body for the Jacobian is supplied with option "jac" (and "hess" for its Jacobian).

Parameters
nameFunction name
bodyC code of the function body, without the enclosing braces
name_inInput names, also the C variable names
name_outOutput names, also the C variable names
sparsity_inSparsity of each input; all scalar when omitted
sparsity_outSparsity of each output; all scalar when omitted
optsOptions; "compiler", "jit_options", "buffered", "jac", "hess" and the common Function options

Example (not run here because it invokes a compiler): f = Function.jit("f", "r[0] = x[0]*x[0] + y[0];", ["x", "y"], ["r"]) gives a function f:(x,y)->(r) that evaluates like any other Function.

See also
external

Function casadi::Function::map ( casadi_int  n,
const std::string &  parallelization = "serial" 
) const
inherited

For f:(a, p)->(s) the result is F:(A, P)->(S) with A = horzcat(a0, ..., a_(n-1)), the same for P, and S = horzcat(f(a0, p0), ..., f(a_(n-1), p_(n-1))). Every input and output is widened to n times its number of columns; when calling, a non-widened argument is repeated for all evaluations. The graph size and construction time are independent of n. For n == 1 the function itself is returned; n < 1 raises "Degenerate map operation".

Parameters
nNumber of evaluations
parallelizationHow the evaluations are run: "serial" (a Map node evaluated in a loop; cached, so repeated calls return the same object), "openmp" (OpenMP parallel loop, requires an OpenMP build), "thread" (std::thread per evaluation), "unroll" (n explicit calls in an MXFunction), "inline" (like unroll with the calls inlined). Other values raise an error.
max_num_threadsWith "thread" or "openmp": split the n evaluations into at most this many parallel chunks, each a serial map

>>> x = SX.sym("x"); p = SX.sym("p")
>>> f = Function("f", [x, p], [p*x**2], ["x", "p"], ["y"])
>>> F = f.map(3)
>>> F
Function(map3_f:(x[1x3],p[1x3])->(y[1x3]) Map)
>>> F(DM([[1, 2, 3]]), 2)
DM([[2, 8, 18]])
>>> f.map(4, "thread", 2)
Function(threadmap2_map2_f:(x[1x4],p[1x4])->(y[1x4]) ThreadMap)
>>> f.map(3, "unroll")
Function(f_3:(x[1x3],p[1x3])->(y[1x3]) MXFunction)
>>> f.map(1) is f, f.map(1).name()
(False, 'f')

◆ mapaccum() [1/6]

Function casadi::Function::mapaccum ( casadi_int  N,
const Dict &  opts = Dict() 
) const
inherited

as inputs

The first n_accum inputs are accumulators: in every step they take the value of the first n_accum outputs of the previous step. For a step f:(x, u)->(x_next, y) the result is F:(x0, U)->(X, Y) with U = horzcat(u0, ..., u_(N-1)), X = horzcat(x1, ..., x_N), Y = horzcat(y0, ..., y_(N-1)) and x_(k+1), y_k = f(x_k, u_k). Non-accumulated inputs and all outputs are stacked horizontally over the N steps; the accumulator inputs keep their original shape. An accumulator output may be wider than its input (e.g. 1-by-2 feeding a 1-by-1 input): only the last columns are fed back.

Compared with writing the loop in the host language the construction is much faster and the graph is a tower of nested unrolled loops of at most base iterations (option "base", default 10; -1 unrolls completely). This keeps memory use proportional to base rather than N at a small evaluation cost.

The overloads differ in how accumulators are selected: a count n_accum (default 1), or explicit index/name lists accum_in and accum_out of equal length that may pick arbitrary inputs and outputs. The unnamed overload names the result "mapaccum_" + name(). fold is mapaccum returning only the final accumulator state.

Parameters
nameName of the result
NNumber of steps, must be positive
n_accumNumber of leading inputs/outputs that are accumulated; at most min(n_in, n_out)
opts"base" plus options for the resulting MXFunction

>>> x = SX.sym("x"); u = SX.sym("u")
>>> step = Function("step", [x, u], [x + u, x*u], ["x", "u"], ["x_next", "y"])
>>> F = step.mapaccum(3)
>>> F
Function(mapaccum_step:(x,u[1x3])->(x_next[1x3],y[1x3]) MXFunction)
>>> F(1, DM([[1, 2, 3]]))
(DM([[2, 4, 7]]), DM([[1, 4, 12]]))
>>> step.mapaccum("F", 3, ["x"], ["x_next"])
Function(F:(x,u[1x3])->(x_next[1x3],y[1x3]) MXFunction)
>>> step.fold(3)
Function(fold_step:(x,u[1x3])->(x_next,y[1x3]) MXFunction)
>>> step.fold(3)(1, DM([[1, 2, 3]]))
(DM(7), DM([[1, 4, 12]]))
>>> try:
...   step.mapaccum(0)
... except RuntimeError as e:
...   print("mapaccum: N must be positive" in str(e))
True

as inputs

The first n_accum inputs are accumulators: in every step they take the value of the first n_accum outputs of the previous step. For a step f:(x, u)->(x_next, y) the result is F:(x0, U)->(X, Y) with U = horzcat(u0, ..., u_(N-1)), X = horzcat(x1, ..., x_N), Y = horzcat(y0, ..., y_(N-1)) and x_(k+1), y_k = f(x_k, u_k). Non-accumulated inputs and all outputs are stacked horizontally over the N steps; the accumulator inputs keep their original shape. An accumulator output may be wider than its input (e.g. 1-by-2 feeding a 1-by-1 input): only the last columns are fed back.

Compared with writing the loop in the host language the construction is much faster and the graph is a tower of nested unrolled loops of at most base iterations (option "base", default 10; -1 unrolls completely). This keeps memory use proportional to base rather than N at a small evaluation cost.

The overloads differ in how accumulators are selected: a count n_accum (default 1), or explicit index/name lists accum_in and accum_out of equal length that may pick arbitrary inputs and outputs. The unnamed overload names the result "mapaccum_" + name(). fold is mapaccum returning only the final accumulator state.

◆ mx_in() [1/3]

const std::vector< MX > casadi::Function::mx_in ( ) const
inherited

Convenient for calling the function symbolically or for building a wrapper: f(f.mx_in()) is an MX expression of the outputs. Each call creates new symbols; they are not the symbols the function was constructed from. All inputs (no argument), one by index, or one by name.

>>> f = Function("f", [SX.sym("a"), SX.sym("B", Sparsity.diag(2))], [SX(0)],
...              ["a", "B"], ["r"])
>>> f.sx_in()
[SX(a), SX(
[[B_0, 00],
 [00, B_1]])]
>>> f.mx_in(1), f.mx_in("a").shape
(MX(B), (1, 1))
>>> f.sx_out(), f.mx_out(0)
([SX(r)], MX(r))


>> a = SX.sym('a'); B = SX.sym('B', Sparsity.diag(2));
>> f = Function('f', {a, B}, {SX(0)}, {'a', 'B'}, {'r'});
>> in = f.sx_in(); disp(in{1}), disp(in{2})
a
[[B_0, 00],
 [00, B_1]]
>> f.mx_in(1), size(f.mx_in('a'))
B
1 1
>> out = f.sx_out(); disp(out{1}), disp(f.mx_out(0))
r
r


julia> a = ca.SX.sym("a"); B = ca.SX.sym("B", ca.Sparsity.diag(2));
julia> f = ca.Function("f", [a, B], [ca.SX(0)], ["a", "B"], ["r"]);
julia> a_in, B_in = ca.sx_in(f);
julia> a_in
SX(a)
julia> B_in
SX(
[[B_0, 00],
 [00, B_1]])
julia> ca.mx_in(f, 1), size(ca.mx_in(f, "a"))
(B, (1, 1))
julia> ca.sx_out(f), ca.mx_out(f, 0)
(SX[r], r)

◆ n_instructions()

casadi_int casadi::Function::n_instructions ( ) const
inherited

The algorithm is the sequence of operations evaluated for a call, including the input and output instructions; instruction_id, instruction_input, instruction_output, instruction_constant and instruction_MX inspect them by index. Other classes raise.

>>> x = SX.sym("x"); y = SX.sym("y")
>>> f = Function("f", [x, y], [x*y + 1])
>>> f.n_instructions()
6
>>> for k in range(f.n_instructions()):
...   print(f.instruction_id(k), f.instruction_input(k), f.instruction_output(k))
45 [0, 0] [0]
45 [1, 0] [1]
3 [0, 1] [0]
44 [] [1]
1 [0, 1] [0]
46 [0] [0, 0]
>>> f.instruction_id(3) == OP_CONST, f.instruction_constant(3)
(True, 1.0)


>> x = SX.sym('x'); y = SX.sym('y');
>> f = Function('f', {x, y}, {x*y + 1});
>> f.n_instructions()
6
>> arrayfun(@(k) f.instruction_id(k), 0:5)
45 45 3 44 1 46
>> f.instruction_input(2), f.instruction_output(2)
0 1
0
>> f.instruction_id(3) == OP_CONST, f.instruction_constant(3)
1
1


julia> x = ca.SX.sym("x"); y = ca.SX.sym("y");
julia> f = ca.Function("f", [x, y], [x*y + 1]);
julia> ca.n_instructions(f)
6
julia> for k in 0:ca.n_instructions(f)-1
           println(ca.instruction_id(f, k), " ", ca.instruction_input(f, k), " ",
                   ca.instruction_output(f, k))
       end
45 [0, 0] [0]
45 [1, 0] [1]
3 [0, 1] [0]
44 Int64[] [1]
1 [0, 1] [0]
46 [0] [0, 0]
julia> ca.instruction_id(f, 3) == ca.OP_CONST, ca.instruction_constant(f, 3)
(true, 1.0)

◆ name_in() [1/2]

const std::vector< std::string > & casadi::Function::name_in ( ) const
inherited

Names come from the constructor; when none were given they are i0, i1, ... Solver objects have fixed schemes, e.g. x0, p, lbx, ubx, lbg, ubg, lam_x0, lam_g0 for nlpsol.

>>> x = SX.sym("x"); y = SX.sym("y")
>>> Function("f", [x, y], [x+y]).name_in()
['i0', 'i1']
>>> f = Function("f", [x, y], [x+y], ["x", "y"], ["r"])
>>> f.name_in(), f.name_in(1), f.name_out()
(['x', 'y'], 'y', ['r'])


>> x = SX.sym('x'); y = SX.sym('y');
>> Function('f', {x, y}, {x+y}).name_in()
i0
i1
>> f = Function('f', {x, y}, {x+y}, {'x', 'y'}, {'r'});
>> f.name_in(), f.name_in(1), f.name_out()
x
y
y
r


julia> x = ca.SX.sym("x"); y = ca.SX.sym("y");
julia> ca.name_in(ca.Function("f", [x, y], [x + y]))
2-element Vector{String}:
 "i0"
 "i1"
julia> f = ca.Function("f", [x, y], [x + y], ["x", "y"], ["r"]);
julia> ca.name_in(f), ca.name_in(f, 1), ca.name_out(f)
(["x", "y"], "y", ["r"])

◆ nnz_in() [1/3]

casadi_int casadi::Function::nnz_in ( ) const
inherited

Without argument, the sum over all inputs. The nonzero count is what numerical evaluation reads for the input; it is smaller than numel_in for sparse inputs.

>>> f = Function("f", [SX.sym("x", 2), SX.sym("D", Sparsity.diag(3))], [SX(1)])
>>> f.nnz_in(0), f.nnz_in(1), f.nnz_in()
(2, 3, 5)
>>> f.numel_in(0), f.numel_in(1), f.numel_in()
(2, 9, 11)


>> f = Function('f', {SX.sym('x', 2), SX.sym('D', Sparsity.diag(3))}, {SX(1)});
>> fprintf('%d %d %d\n', f.nnz_in(0), f.nnz_in(1), f.nnz_in())
2 3 5
>> fprintf('%d %d %d\n', f.numel_in(0), f.numel_in(1), f.numel_in())
2 9 11


julia> D = ca.SX.sym("D", ca.Sparsity.diag(3));
julia> f = ca.Function("f", [ca.SX.sym("x", 2), D], [ca.SX(1)]);
julia> ca.nnz_in(f, 0), ca.nnz_in(f, 1), ca.nnz_in(f)
(2, 3, 5)
julia> ca.numel_in(f, 0), ca.numel_in(f, 1), ca.numel_in(f)
(2, 9, 11)

See also
nnz_out, numel_in, sparsity_in

◆ nz_from_in()

std::vector< double > casadi::Function::nz_from_in ( const std::vector< DM > &  arg) const
inherited

nonzeros

nz_from_in flattens a list of n_in() DM arguments (shape rules as in call) into the concatenated nonzeros, in input order and column-major within each input; nz_to_in does the reverse, the list must have exactly nnz_in() entries. nz_from_out and nz_to_out do the same for the outputs with nnz_out(). This is the memory layout that generated C code and FunctionBuffer use.

>>> f = Function("f", [SX.sym("x"), SX.sym("D", Sparsity.diag(2))], [SX(0)])
>>> f.nz_from_in([1, DM([[2, 0], [0, 3]])])
[1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
>>> f.nz_to_in([1, 2, 3])
[DM(1), DM(
[[2, 00],
 [00, 3]])]
>>> try:
...   f.nz_to_in([1, 2])
... except RuntimeError as e:
...   print("Dimension mismatch. Expecting 3, got 2" in str(e))
True


>> f = Function('f', {SX.sym('x'), SX.sym('D', Sparsity.diag(2))}, {SX(0)});
>> f.nz_from_in({1, DM([2, 0; 0, 3])})
1 2 3
>> arg = f.nz_to_in([1, 2, 3]); disp(arg{1}), disp(arg{2})
1
[[2, 00],
 [00, 3]]
>> try, f.nz_to_in([1, 2]); catch e, disp(contains(e.message, 'Expecting 3, got 2')); end
1

◆ reverse()

Function casadi::Function::reverse ( casadi_int  nadj) const
inherited

The result is named adj<nadj>_<name> and has n_in + n_out + n_out inputs: the original inputs, the original outputs (out_<name>) and the adjoint seeds adj_<output>, each with nadj times the columns of the output. Its n_in outputs adj_<input> are the adjoint sensitivities, nadj stacked horizontally. Falls back to the full Jacobian when the class has no reverse mode; raises when it has no derivatives at all. Results are cached while alive. nadj must be positive.

>>> x = SX.sym("x"); y = SX.sym("y", 2)
>>> f = Function("f", [x, y], [x*y, sin(x)], ["x", "y"], ["r", "s"])
>>> R = f.reverse(1)
>>> R
Function(adj1_f:(x,y[2],out_r[2x1,0nz],out_s[1x1,0nz],adj_r[2],adj_s)->(adj_x,adj_y[2])
SXFunction)
>>> R(1, [2, 3], 0, 0, [1, 1], 0)
(DM(5), DM([1, 1]))


>> x = SX.sym('x'); y = SX.sym('y', 2);
>> f = Function('f', {x, y}, {x*y, sin(x)}, {'x', 'y'}, {'r', 's'});
>> R = f.reverse(1); disp(R)
adj1_f:(x,y[2],out_r[2x1,0nz],out_s[1x1,0nz],adj_r[2],adj_s)->(adj_x,adj_y[2]) SXFunction
>> [adj_x, adj_y] = R(1, [2; 3], 0, 0, [1; 1], 0); disp(adj_x), disp(adj_y)

[1, 1]

Writes a serialization of the function to fname (conventionally with the extension .casadi). The file is portable across platforms and languages (Python, MATLAB, C++); it is compatible across CasADi versions as far as the serialization format allows.

Parameters
fnameFile name
optsSerializer options, e.g. "debug"

>>> x = SX.sym("x")
>>> f = Function("f", [x], [x**2])

>>> g = Function.load("f.casadi")

(Function(f:(i0)->(o0) SXFunction), DM(9))
>>> os.remove("f.casadi")

◆ serialize() [1/3]

std::string casadi::Function::serialize ( const Dict &  opts = Dict()) const
inherited

Any Function can be serialized, including solvers and functions with embedded calls; a just-in-time compiled function is stored according to option "jit_serialize". The string is binary-safe text; it is also what the Python pickle protocol and MATLAB save use.

Parameters
opts"debug" (bool) adds consistency markers to the stream

>>> x = SX.sym("x")
>>> f = Function("f", [x], [sin(x)], ["x"], ["y"])
>>> s = f.serialize()
>>> g = Function.deserialize(s)
>>> g, g(1)
(Function(f:(x)->(y) SXFunction), DM(0.841471))


>> x = SX.sym('x');

◆ size1_in() [1/2]

casadi_int casadi::Function::size1_in ( casadi_int  ind) const
inherited

size1_in is the number of rows, size2_in the number of columns and size_in the pair (rows, columns). The input is selected by index or by name; an unknown name raises an error listing the available names, an index out of range raises an error.

>>> f = Function("f", [SX.sym("A", 2, 3), SX.sym("b", 2)], [SX(0)], ["A", "b"], ["c"])
>>> f.size_in(0), f.size1_in("A"), f.size2_in("A")
((2, 3), 2, 3)
>>> f.size_in("b")
(2, 1)
>>> try:
...   f.size_in("nope")
... except RuntimeError as e:
...   print("Available names are: [A, b]" in str(e))
True


>> f = Function('f', {SX.sym('A', 2, 3), SX.sym('b', 2)}, {SX(0)}, {'A', 'b'}, {'c'});
>> disp(f.size_in(0)), fprintf('%d %d\n', f.size1_in('A'), f.size2_in('A'))
2 3
2 3
>> f.size_in('b')
2 1
>> try, f.size_in('nope'); catch e, disp(contains(e.message, 'Available names')); end
1


julia> A = ca.SX.sym("A", 2, 3); b = ca.SX.sym("b", 2);
julia> f = ca.Function("f", [A, b], [ca.SX(0)], ["A", "b"], ["c"]);

((2, 3), 2, 3)

(2, 1)
julia> try

size1_in is the number of rows, size2_in the number of columns and size_in the pair (rows, columns). The input is selected by index or by name; an unknown name raises an error listing the available names, an index out of range raises an error.

>>> f = Function("f", [SX.sym("A", 2, 3), SX.sym("b", 2)], [SX(0)], ["A", "b"], ["c"])
>>> f.size_in(0), f.size1_in("A"), f.size2_in("A")
((2, 3), 2, 3)
>>> f.size_in("b")
(2, 1)
>>> try:
...   f.size_in("nope")
... except RuntimeError as e:
...   print("Available names are: [A, b]" in str(e))
True


>> f = Function('f', {SX.sym('A', 2, 3), SX.sym('b', 2)}, {SX(0)}, {'A', 'b'}, {'c'});
>> disp(f.size_in(0)), fprintf('%d %d\n', f.size1_in('A'), f.size2_in('A'))
2 3
2 3
>> f.size_in('b')
2 1
>> try, f.size_in('nope'); catch e, disp(contains(e.message, 'Available names')); end
1

(2, 1)

◆ slice()

Function casadi::Function::slice ( const std::string &  name,
const std::vector< casadi_int > &  order_in,
const std::vector< casadi_int > &  order_out,
const Dict &  opts = Dict() 
) const
inherited

The expressions are unchanged; only the lists of inputs and outputs are rearranged. Indices may be repeated or omitted. An omitted input that an output depends on makes the result have free variables (construction then fails unless "allow_free" is in opts). Classes other than SXFunction and MXFunction are wrapped first.

Parameters
nameName of the result
order_inIndices of the original inputs to keep, in the new order
order_outIndices of the original outputs to keep, in the new order
optsOptions for the new function

>>> x = SX.sym("x"); y = SX.sym("y")
>>> f = Function("f", [x, y], [x + y, x - y, 2*x], ["x", "y"], ["a", "b", "c"])
>>> g = f.slice("g", [1, 0], [2, 0])
>>> g, g(1, 2)
(Function(g:(y,x)->(c,a) SXFunction), (DM(4), DM(3)))
>>> f.slice("h", [0], [2])
Function(h:(x)->(c) SXFunction)


>> x = SX.sym('x'); y = SX.sym('y');
>> f = Function('f', {x, y}, {x + y, x - y, 2*x}, {'x', 'y'}, {'a', 'b', 'c'});
>> g = f.slice('g', [1, 0], [2, 0]); disp(g)
g:(y,x)->(c,a) SXFunction
>> [c, a] = g(1, 2); disp(c), disp(a)
4
3
>> f.slice('h', 0, 2)
h:(x)->(c) SXFunction


julia> x = ca.SX.sym("x"); y = ca.SX.sym("y");
julia> f = ca.Function("f", [x, y], [x + y, x - y, 2x], ["x", "y"], ["a", "b", "c"]);
julia> g = ca.slice(f, "g", [1, 0], [2, 0]);
julia> println(g); g(1, 2)
g:(y,x)->(c,a) SXFunction
(4, 3)
julia> ca.slice(f, "h", [0], [2])
Function(h:(x)->(c) SXFunction)

◆ sparsity_in() [1/2]

const Sparsity & casadi::Function::sparsity_in ( casadi_int  ind) const

Numerical arguments are projected onto this pattern before evaluation: entries outside it are dropped silently. Symbolic inputs keep the pattern of the expression passed to the constructor.

>>> f = Function("f", [SX.sym("D", Sparsity.diag(2))], [SX(0)], ["D"], ["r"])

Sparsity(2x2,2nz)
>>> f.sparsity_in("D").is_diag()
True
>>> f.sparsity_out(0)
Sparsity(1x1)

◆ stats()

Dict casadi::Function::stats ( int  mem = 0) const
inherited

The content depends on the class: solvers report e.g. "success", "return_status", "iter_count"; with option "record_time" every function reports "t_wall_total", "t_proc_total" and "n_call_total". Raises an error when the function has not been evaluated numerically yet.

Parameters
memMemory object (from checkout) whose statistics to return; 0 is the memory used by ordinary calls

>>> x = SX.sym("x")
>>> f = Function("f", [x], [x**2], {"record_time": True})
>>> try:
...   f.stats()
... except RuntimeError as e:
...   print("first evaluate it numerically" in str(e))
True
>>> r = f(2)
>>> sorted(f.stats().keys())
['n_call_total', 't_proc_total', 't_wall_total']


>> x = SX.sym('x');
>> f = Function('f', {x}, {x^2}, struct('record_time', true));
>> try, f.stats(); catch e, disp(contains(e.message, 'first evaluate it numerically')); end
1
>> r = f(2); disp(strjoin(sort(fieldnames(f.stats()))', ' '))
n_call_total t_proc_total t_wall_total


julia> x = ca.SX.sym("x");
julia> f = ca.Function("f", [x], [x^2], Dict("record_time" => true));
julia> try
           ca.stats(f)
       catch e
           println(occursin("first evaluate it numerically", sprint(showerror, e)))
       end
true
julia> r = f(2);
julia> sort(collect(keys(ca.stats(f))))
3-element Vector{String}:
 "n_call_total"
 "t_proc_total"
 "t_wall_total"

Convenient for calling the function symbolically or for building a wrapper: f(f.mx_in()) is an MX expression of the outputs. Each call creates new symbols; they are not the symbols the function was constructed from. All inputs (no argument), one by index, or one by name.

>>> f = Function("f", [SX.sym("a"), SX.sym("B", Sparsity.diag(2))], [SX(0)],
...              ["a", "B"], ["r"])
>>> f.sx_in()
[SX(a), SX(
[[B_0, 00],
 [00, B_1]])]
>>> f.mx_in(1), f.mx_in("a").shape
(MX(B), (1, 1))
>>> f.sx_out(), f.mx_out(0)
([SX(r)], MX(r))


>> a = SX.sym('a'); B = SX.sym('B', Sparsity.diag(2));
>> f = Function('f', {a, B}, {SX(0)}, {'a', 'B'}, {'r'});
>> in = f.sx_in(); disp(in{1}), disp(in{2})
a
[[B_0, 00],
 [00, B_1]]
>> f.mx_in(1), size(f.mx_in('a'))
B
1 1
>> out = f.sx_out(); disp(out{1}), disp(f.mx_out(0))
r
r

(B, (1, 1))

◆ transform() [1/4]

Function casadi::Function::transform ( const Dict &  opts = Dict()) const
inherited

Only defined for SXFunction and MXFunction. The result has the same signature, names and options; only the expression graph differs.

The dict form runs a single "simplify" pass whose tasks are selected with boolean options, all defaulting to on except combine_terms:

  • empty_inputs: an input whose symbols do not occur in any output is replaced by an all-zero sparse matrix of the same shape (its nnz becomes 0)
  • cse: common subexpression elimination
  • ref_count: drop unreferenced nodes, repeated until a fixed point
  • const_folding: evaluate constant subexpressions
  • combine_terms: merge like terms of sums

Unknown keys raise an error.

The passes form runs an explicit list of passes in order. Each pass is a list whose first entry is the verb:

  • ["simplify", task, ...] with tasks from the list above; an integer before a task is its run count (N>0: N times, 0: until the graph stops shrinking)
  • ["expand"]: expand to an SXFunction
  • ["external", library, operation] or [..., opts]: a transform from a plugin library

Here opts accepts only "verbose"; passing the boolean task options raises an error. With "verbose": true the node and instruction counts after each pass are printed.

Parameters
fnameName of the result; defaults to the current name
passesExplicit list of passes
optsDict form: task booleans and "verbose"; passes form: "verbose" only

>>> z = MX.sym("z"); w = MX.sym("w")
>>> f = Function("f", [z, w], [sin(z)*cos(z) + sin(z)*cos(z)], ["z", "w"], ["r"])
>>> f, f.n_instructions()
(Function(f:(z,w)->(r) MXFunction), 9)
>>> g = f.transform()
>>> g, g.n_instructions()
(Function(f:(z,w[1x1,0nz])->(r) MXFunction), 6)
>>> f.transform([["simplify", "cse"]]).n_instructions()
6
>>> f.transform("fe", [["expand"]])
Function(fe:(z,w)->(r) SXFunction)
>>> try:
...   f.transform([["nope"]])
... except RuntimeError as e:
...   print("unknown pass verb" in str(e))
True


>> z = MX.sym('z'); w = MX.sym('w');
>> f = Function('f', {z, w}, {sin(z)*cos(z) + sin(z)*cos(z)}, {'z', 'w'}, {'r'});
>> f, f.n_instructions()
f:(z,w)->(r) MXFunction
9
>> g = f.transform(); disp(g), disp(g.n_instructions())
f:(z,w[1x1,0nz])->(r) MXFunction
6
>> f.transform({{'simplify', 'cse'}}).n_instructions()
6
>> f.transform('fe', {{'expand'}})
fe:(z,w)->(r) SXFunction
>> try, f.transform({{'nope'}}); catch e, disp(contains(e.message, 'unknown pass')); end
1


julia> z = ca.MX.sym("z"); w = ca.MX.sym("w");
julia> f = ca.Function("f", [z, w], [sin(z)*cos(z) + sin(z)*cos(z)], ["z", "w"], ["r"]);
julia> println(f); ca.n_instructions(f)
f:(z,w)->(r) MXFunction
9
julia> g = ca.transform(f);
julia> println(g); ca.n_instructions(g)
f:(z,w[1x1,0nz])->(r) MXFunction
6
julia> ca.n_instructions(ca.transform(f, [["simplify", "cse"]]))
6
julia> ca.transform(f, "fe", [["expand"]])
Function(fe:(z,w)->(r) SXFunction)
julia> try
           ca.transform(f, [["nope"]])
       catch e

       end

◆ uses_output()

bool casadi::Callback::uses_output ( ) const
virtual

Derivative functions obtained from get_jacobian/get_forward/get_reverse receive the nominal outputs as extra inputs. When this returns false (default) those inputs are passed as empty (all-zero sparsity) placeholders; return true to receive the actual output values, e.g. to reuse them in the derivative computation.

>>> class Sq(Callback):
...   def __init__(self, name, opts={}):
...     Callback.__init__(self)

◆ which_depends()

std::vector< bool > casadi::Function::which_depends ( const std::string &  s_in,
const std::vector< std::string > &  s_out,
casadi_int  order = 1,
bool  tr = false 
) const
inherited

Returns one boolean per nonzero of input s_in: true when at least one of the outputs s_out depends on that entry (order 1) or depends on it nonlinearly (order 2). With tr true the relation is flipped: one boolean per nonzero of the vertically concatenated outputs, true when it depends on any entry of s_in. The analysis is structural (it follows the graph, not the values).

Parameters
s_inName of one input
s_outNames of the outputs to inspect
order1 (any dependence) or 2 (nonlinear dependence); other values raise
trTranspose the relation, see above

>>> x = SX.sym("x"); y = SX.sym("y", 2)
>>> f = Function("f", [x, y], [x*y[0], y[1]**2 + x, 3], ["x", "y"], ["a", "b", "c"])
>>> f.which_depends("y", ["a", "b"])
[True, True]
>>> f.which_depends("y", ["a", "b"], 2)
[False, True]
>>> f.which_depends("y", ["a", "b", "c"], 1, True)
[True, True, False]
>>> f.which_depends("x", ["a"], 2)
[False]


>> x = SX.sym('x'); y = SX.sym('y', 2);
>> f = Function('f', {x, y}, {x*y(1), y(2)^2 + x, 3}, {'x', 'y'}, {'a', 'b', 'c'});
>> f.which_depends('y', {'a', 'b'})
1 1
>> f.which_depends('y', {'a', 'b'}, 2)
0 1
>> f.which_depends('y', {'a', 'b', 'c'}, 1, true)
1 1 0
>> f.which_depends('x', {'a'}, 2)
0


julia> x = ca.SX.sym("x"); y = ca.SX.sym("y", 2);
julia> f = ca.Function("f", [x, y], [x*y[1], y[2]^2 + x, 3], ["x", "y"], ["a", "b", "c"]);
julia> ca.which_depends(f, "y", ["a", "b"])
2-element Vector{Bool}:
 1
 1
julia> ca.which_depends(f, "y", ["a", "b"], 2)
2-element Vector{Bool}:
 0
 1
julia> ca.which_depends(f, "y", ["a", "b", "c"], 1, true)
3-element Vector{Bool}:
 1
 1
 0
julia> ca.which_depends(f, "x", ["a"], 2)
1-element Vector{Bool}:
 0

◆ wrap() [1/2]

Function casadi::Function::wrap ( ) const
inherited

The wrapper has the same signature and names, carries over the derivative options (ad_weight, ad_weight_sp, max_num_dir, is_diff_in/out, derivative_of) and is cached by name. Classes without their own derivative or slice implementation use it internally; it is also a way to give any function a plain MX graph.

Parameters
nameName of the wrapper; defaults to "wrap_" + name()

>>> x = SX.sym("x")
>>> f = Function("f", [x], [sin(x)], ["x"], ["y"])
>>> w = f.wrap()
>>> w, w.n_instructions(), w.get_function()
(Function(wrap_f:(x)->(y) MXFunction), 3, ['f'])
>>> f.wrap("g").name()
'g'


>> x = SX.sym('x');
>> f = Function('f', {x}, {sin(x)}, {'x'}, {'y'});
>> w = f.wrap(); disp(w), disp(w.n_instructions()), disp(w.get_function())
wrap_f:(x)->(y) MXFunction
3
f
>> f.wrap('g').name()
g


julia> x = ca.SX.sym("x");
julia> f = ca.Function("f", [x], [sin(x)], ["x"], ["y"]);
julia> w = ca.wrap(f);
julia> println(w); ca.n_instructions(w), ca.get_function(w)
wrap_f:(x)->(y) MXFunction
(3, ["f"])
julia> ca.name(ca.wrap(f, "g"))
"g"

See also
wrap_as_needed, expand

◆ wrap_as_needed() [1/2]

Function casadi::Function::wrap_as_needed ( const Dict &  opts) const
inherited

Like wrap, but the wrapper is built with opts (merged with the derivative options of this function) and is not cached. The named overload returns this function itself when opts is empty and name equals its current name; the unnamed overload always wraps, under the name "wrap_" + name().

>>> x = SX.sym("x")
>>> f = Function("f", [x], [sin(x)])
>>> f.wrap_as_needed("f", {}).class_name(), f.wrap_as_needed({}).class_name()
('SXFunction', 'MXFunction')
>>> f.wrap_as_needed("g", {"ad_weight": 1}).name()
'g'


>> x = SX.sym('x');
>> f = Function('f', {x}, {sin(x)});
>> f.wrap_as_needed('f', struct()).class_name()
SXFunction
>> f.wrap_as_needed(struct()).class_name()
MXFunction
>> f.wrap_as_needed('g', struct('ad_weight', 1)).name()
g


julia> x = ca.SX.sym("x");
julia> f = ca.Function("f", [x], [sin(x)]);
julia> ca.class_name(ca.wrap_as_needed(f, "f", Dict()))
"SXFunction"
julia> ca.class_name(ca.wrap_as_needed(f, Dict()))
"MXFunction"
julia> ca.name(ca.wrap_as_needed(f, "g", Dict("ad_weight" => 1)))
"g"
